title: NEURA unveils a lighter 4NE1 Gen 4 humanoid as the TUM RoboGym opens near Munich
summary: NEURA says its 4NE1 Gen 4 humanoid is 20% lighter and being readied for series production; it launched at the new TUM RoboGym near Munich Airport.
body: Short answer: NEURA Robotics unveiled 4NE1 Gen 4 on 22 October 2026, a new generation of its humanoid robot that the company says is 20 percent lighter than the previous version and is being prepared for series production. The launch coincided with the opening of the TUM RoboGym, a robot training and research centre near Munich Airport run with the Technical University of Munich (TUM), according to both organisations.

According to NEURA, Gen 4 has a slimmer body covered in a black textile outer skin, upgraded hands for finer gripping, and what the company calls Smart Limbs, with reflexes built into each limb. It runs Neuron AI, which NEURA describes as a Perception-Language-Action model that combines vision, touch, force, sound and the robot's own state; the company's example is sensing whether a fastener has clicked into place. Interesting Engineering reported the same details on 23 October.

NEURA says the RoboGym covers more than 2,300 square metres at the LabCampus site. TUM says around 100 humanoid and service robots will initially learn skills there in 48 training cells, with an early focus on industrial applications and intralogistics, and that the data will flow into a curated cloud data lake for research. According to NEURA, partners from more than ten industries, including automotive, pharmaceuticals, logistics, agriculture and care, have been training workflows at the site since September, on tasks such as handling boxes, filling bottles and loading wooden parts.

The partners describe an initial three-year initiative with a combined investment of about €17 million, of which NEURA says it is contributing about €11 million. NEURA says Munich is the first of a planned network of NEURA Gyms, with more being set up in Europe, the United States and China and another in Germany with RWTH Aachen. The company says the robot was also shown at NVIDIA's GTC event in Berlin, where Agile Robots presented its Agile ONE SN humanoid. The announcements do not give a price or delivery date for 4NE1 Gen 4.
analysis: Opinion: Launching a robot together with a training facility reflects a wider industry view that real-world physical data, not only hardware, is what holds humanoids back. Whether Gen 4's claimed improvements lead to dependable factory work will depend on results from sites like the RoboGym, and none have been published yet.
disclaimer: Specifications, plans and investment figures are NEURA's and TUM's own statements and have not been independently verified. This is not investment advice.

title: Generative Bionics plans a 5,000 m² humanoid training "data factory" in Italy with AMD
summary: Generative Bionics says it will build a three-site Physical AI Data Factory network, starting with a 5,000 m² Italian hub due by Q4 2027, using AMD compute.
body: Short answer: Italian humanoid developer Generative Bionics announced on 21 October 2026 that it plans a network of three "Physical AI Data Factory" sites to train humanoid robots, starting with a 5,000-square-metre hub in Italy that it expects to be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027, with AMD as its AI infrastructure partner, according to the company's press release.

The company says fleets of its GENE.01 humanoid will carry out industrial tasks continuously in reproduced real-world work environments chosen with industrial partners, generating data to train what it calls World Action Models. Each environment will also be rebuilt as a digital twin so tasks can be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, conditions and failure modes, and models trained in simulation will return to the physical robots for validation, a loop Generative Bionics calls real-to-sim-to-real.

According to the release, AMD Helios rack-scale systems will provide the compute for processing physical and synthetic data, training models and running simulations. A second site is planned elsewhere in Europe and a third to serve global markets. Generative Bionics says the first hub will be Europe's largest physical AI training facility for humanoid robots; that is the company's own description. Robotics & Automation News reported the plan on 23 October.

Generative Bionics presents the project as supporting European control over humanoid data, models and know-how. The company says AMD Ventures took part in its €70 million seed round led by CDP Venture Capital, and that AMD compute already runs on board GENE.01. Other developers are also combining real and simulated training, including NEURA with its new TUM RoboGym and Unitree with its Rehearsal project.
analysis: Opinion: Dedicated robot data-collection sites are becoming a common bet among European humanoid developers. The timeline is long, with the first hub not due until late 2027, and the announcement gives no cost figure for the network.
disclaimer: Plans, timelines and the "largest" description are Generative Bionics' own statements and have not been independently verified. Funding details are as stated by the company. This is not investment advice.

title: AiMOGA opens worldwide pre-orders for Mobo, a 0.9 m family companion humanoid
summary: AiMOGA Robotics says it has opened global pre-orders for Mobo, a 0.9-metre home companion humanoid with 22 degrees of freedom; no price was announced.
body: Short answer: AiMOGA Robotics, based in Wuhu, China, said on 22 October 2026 that it has unveiled Mobo, its first consumer family companion humanoid, and opened pre-orders worldwide, according to a company press release. The announcement does not state a price or delivery date.

According to AiMOGA, Mobo is 0.9 metres tall, has 22 degrees of freedom and supports more than 20 languages. The company is aiming it at households: object recognition, questions and answers, storytelling and English practice for children, and conversation and reminders for older family members. AiMOGA says the robot recognises family members using face ID and keeps memories linked to each person.

Mobo runs on MoAgent, which AiMOGA describes as its embodied-intelligence agent, with a "dual-brain" design for planning and fast responses and a world model to check whether tasks have been completed. The company says the robot can handle up to 16 tasks in parallel with an interruption response time under 0.2 seconds, and that eligible data is de-identified on the device before it is used for cloud learning. These figures have not been independently tested.

AiMOGA says more than 10,000 prospective users have shown interest since Mobo's debut at the World Robot Conference in August 2026. More broadly, the company says it has sold more than 3,000 robots across over 60 countries and regions, and plans 300 experience centres worldwide and a robot-leasing brand starting in Wuhu, drawing on the manufacturing and sales resources of carmaker Chery.
analysis: Opinion: Home companion humanoids are still an early, untested category compared with the factory robots that dominate most humanoid news. Until a price, shipping date and independent reviews are available, it is hard to judge how Mobo will perform in real homes.
disclaimer: All specifications, sales and interest figures are AiMOGA's own claims from a press release and have not been independently verified.

title: Chinese humanoid makers seek factory and cafe trials in South Korea
summary: UBTech, Anyverse Dynamics and other Chinese firms are pursuing trials in South Korea as Seoul proposes 3.1 trillion won for physical AI, Korea Times reports.
body: Short answer: Chinese humanoid robot makers including UBTech, Anyverse Dynamics, AgiBot and Unitree are trying to win work in South Korea through factory trials and commercial projects as Seoul raises spending on physical AI, The Korea Times reported on 23 October 2026, in an article also published by the South China Morning Post.

According to the report, UBTech announced in July that it would trial humanoids on a Korean automotive parts line with local partner Duksan JM Robotics and parts maker AJIN Industrial, and a UBTech executive said several models are undergoing on-site tests in the country, without giving details. The same executive said Seoul's Galaxy Robot Park, a robot-themed entertainment venue, bought UBTech's U1 model for around 170,000 yuan (about $25,000). Beijing start-up Anyverse Dynamics told the paper it plans trials in Korean cafes and other service settings in the fourth quarter before moving into manufacturing, and is working on product certification.

Chinese customs data cited in the report show South Korea was China's third-largest export market by value for "intelligent bionic robots" in the first nine months of 2026, at $19.99 million, behind the United States and Japan; the category, introduced this year, covers humanoid robots and robot dogs. The report says Korea's KC certification rules led UBTech to adapt its communication modules and radio settings for the local market.

On policy, the report says the government has proposed 3.1 trillion won (about $2.34 billion) for physical AI in 2027, more than triple this year's figure, and that the industry ministry's M.AX programme targets 500 AI factories by 2030. Korean companies are also active: the paper cites LG Electronics' robot data factory in Seoul, Samsung Electronics' new Robotics eXperience division and Hyundai Motor Group's training of Boston Dynamics' Atlas humanoids in Georgia ahead of a planned 2028 manufacturing deployment. A Counterpoint Research analyst told the paper the lack of locally built humanoids at scale has created an opening for Chinese suppliers, but that they need local customers willing to run proof-of-concept trials. We previously covered Korea's safety-rule exemption for a Robros factory pilot and China's humanoid output and standards push.
analysis: Opinion: South Korea pairs dense manufacturing with an aggressive policy push but few local humanoid suppliers at scale, which makes it a logical test market for Chinese makers. The report points to certification and finding local trial partners as the practical hurdles.
disclaimer: Figures are as reported by The Korea Times and the South China Morning Post, citing company executives, Chinese customs data and government plans; budget figures are proposals. This is not investment advice.

title: Why UCLA's PhoneBot, a small humanoid run by a smartphone, is getting attention
summary: UCLA's open-source PhoneBot uses an Android phone for sensing and computing in a 48 cm biped that its researchers say costs about $400 without the phone.
why: What happened: UCLA's RoMeLa lab described PhoneBot in an October 2026 arXiv preprint, New Atlas covered it on 12 October, and it appeared among X's trending robotics stories on 23 October.

Why it is being discussed: the low estimated parts cost of about $400 excluding the phone, and fully open hardware and software, compared with small research humanoids the paper lists at roughly $3,500 to $13,800 (arXiv, New Atlas).
What to watch: whether others build and extend the open design, and the limits the authors list, including no arms and walking trained only on flat ground.
body: Short answer: PhoneBot is a small open-source humanoid from UCLA's Robotics and Mechanisms Laboratory (RoMeLa) that uses an ordinary Android smartphone as its camera, balance sensor, screen and main computer. The researchers estimate its parts cost at about $400 excluding the phone, according to their arXiv preprint and New Atlas, and the project was among X's trending robotics stories on 23 October 2026.

According to the paper, the robot is 48.3 cm tall, weighs 1.8 kg including the phone, and uses 13 low-cost servo motors: six in each leg plus one that turns the torso. The phone is not wired to the body; it sends joint commands over Wi-Fi to a small onboard computer that drives the motors, which the authors say makes it easier to swap in different phones.

The walking controller was trained in simulation with reinforcement learning, and the team reports demonstrations of walking, following a person using the phone's camera, and standing up from a face-down position. The researchers say they tested the app on four Android phones, including a 2017 Honor 9 and three prepaid models costing about $50 to $80, and that camera-based mapping did not run on the Honor 9. Speech recognition and the language model currently run on a nearby laptop rather than on the robot, the paper says.

The authors also list limitations: PhoneBot has no arms, its walking was trained only for flat ground, and its small motors limit what it can carry. The design files and code are open source and aimed at education and research, according to the project. For another example of low-cost humanoid research, see our report on Berkeley's SuperMimic controller trained on one GPU.
disclaimer: Cost and performance figures are the researchers' own, from a preprint and the project materials; they have not been independently verified. Cost comparisons with other platforms are approximate and not like-for-like.

title: Unitree says it is building "Rehearsal", a self-improving loop for robot software
summary: Unitree's Wang Xingxing said on 22 Oct 2026 the firm is developing "Rehearsal", a loop for robots to write code, test it in simulation and improve (SCMP).
body: Short answer: Unitree founder Wang Xingxing said on 22 October 2026 that the company is developing "Unitree Rehearsal", a "self-evolving" feedback loop designed to let humanoid robots write code, run simulations and improve their real-world performance with less manual programming, the South China Morning Post reported.

SCMP says Wang unveiled the project at a physical AI conference hosted by Unitree in Hangzhou and called it the company's most important initiative of the year. In the system under development, AI would search research papers, write code and test it in simulation before running trials on physical robots.
Humans could still assess performance and give feedback, according to SCMP, but Wang said the ultimate goal is an automated cycle that could greatly speed up the development of robotics algorithms.

PANews, summarising his keynote, reports that Wang said leading AI-model companies have in a sense already achieved self-evolution of models internally, and that the core challenge for embodied AI to have its "ChatGPT moment" is aligning AI model inputs and outputs with real robots. Neither report gives technical details, test results or a release date.
disclaimer: Rehearsal is described as under development, based on a keynote as reported by two outlets. No results have been published in the sources, so its capabilities are unproven.

title: Why Unitree's H2-X "Guardian" video is getting attention
summary: Unitree's H2-X teaser shows martial arts and staged rescue scenes; outlets note it released few specifications and it is unclear how autonomous the demos were.
body: Short answer: Unitree's H2-X "Kung Fu Legend Guardian" teaser video, released on 21 October 2026, has been widely covered because it shows a humanoid performing martial-arts moves and staged security and rescue scenes. Unitree has released few specifications, and outlets note it is unclear how autonomous the demos were.

Interesting Engineering, CNBC-TV18 and TechRadar describe the clip: kicks and punches that dent scrapyard cars, a jump from a platform marked four metres high, and staged scenes in which the robot steps between a woman and a person carrying a weapon, pushes a person away from an approaching car and lifts the front of a vehicle above a dummy.

On X, Unitree described the robot as offering "powerful performance to serve and guard you" with a maximum endurance of approximately eight hours, CNBC-TV18 reports; the on-screen safety text calls the figure standing time and advises staying two to three metres away. Interesting Engineering says the H2-X is based on Unitree's H2, which the company describes as about 1.8 metres tall and 70 kg. No price or release date has been announced, TechRadar and Interesting Engineering report.

Interesting Engineering and CNBC-TV18, the latter citing SCMP, say Unitree has not said whether the actions were autonomous, remotely controlled or pre-programmed. TechRadar calls the video more tech demo than consumer product and says it doubts such a robot could clear consumer certification as a personal bodyguard; that is the outlet's view, not Unitree's.
why: What happened: Unitree published a roughly one-minute promo for the H2-X on 21 October showing martial-arts moves and staged security and rescue scenes (TechRadar, Interesting Engineering).
Why it is being discussed: coverage focuses on how real the capabilities are, noting that autonomy, price and availability were not stated (Interesting Engineering, CNBC-TV18).
What to watch: whether Unitree publishes specifications, availability and how the demos were controlled.
disclaimer: Descriptions of the video and robot come from the company's own promotional material as reported by the outlets cited. We have not tested the robot, and its real-world performance is unverified.

title: Why Figure's nine-day Figure 03 treadmill test is getting attention
summary: Figure CEO Brett Adcock said a Figure 03 robot walked 348 miles over nine days on a treadmill; outlets note power and interruption details are unclear.
body: Short answer: Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock said on X on 19 October 2026 that a Figure 03 humanoid had walked on a treadmill for nine straight days, covering 348 miles and about 1.2 million steps in a test he said began as a side project to stress the robot for failures. The figures come from the company's CEO and have not been independently verified.

Interesting Engineering reports that a time-lapse shows the robot walking on a treadmill inside a testing facility with a power cable attached. Adcock's post ended with "Let's see how long it can go", which suggests the run was still going when he posted.

Both Interesting Engineering and TechRepublic note that details are unclear: whether one robot completed the whole run, how power and charging were handled, and whether there were interruptions or maintenance. TechRepublic says the result should not be read as nine days on a single battery charge.

For context, Interesting Engineering and TechRepublic recall Figure's May 2026 livestream of package sorting, which ran for about 200 hours and processed 249,560 packages, with several robots rotating through the task. The treadmill test instead emphasises accumulated walking distance and steps.
why: What happened: Brett Adcock said on 19 October that Figure 03 had walked 348 miles and about 1.2 million steps on a treadmill over nine days (Interesting Engineering, TechRepublic).
Why it is being discussed: Interesting Engineering describes it as a longer stress test meant to expose weaknesses that shorter demos might miss, while both outlets stress what remains unclear.
What to watch: independently verified endurance data, maintenance and uptime figures, and whether the test result is confirmed as a single robot's continuous run.
disclaimer: The test figures were reported by the company's CEO and relayed by news outlets; they have not been independently verified.

title: Tesla targets end of 2027 for external Optimus deliveries, Musk says
summary: Elon Musk said on Tesla's Q3 2026 earnings call that Tesla expects to start delivering Optimus robots to outside customers around the end of 2027, according to Electrek.
body: Short answer: Elon Musk said on Tesla's Q3 2026 earnings call that Tesla expects to begin delivering Optimus robots to outside customers around the end of 2027, once open issues with the AI, the hardware design and reliability are resolved, according to Electrek's report of the call.

Musk said Tesla has started early Optimus production at its Fremont factory in California, in an area that previously built Model S and Model X cars. He said most of the equipment for a line sized for one million robots a year is in place, but that reaching that pace could take a year or more because the design is still changing.

Asked what was still changing, a Tesla Optimus engineer pointed to the robot's hand and to custom gears with outstanding reliability concerns, Electrek reported. On AI, Musk said Tesla plans to build 10,000 to 20,000 robots to practise tasks in a programme it calls the "Optimus Academy", and to fit its AI5 chip to Optimus around April 2027.

Tesla expects its first outside customers to use Optimus for industrial work that is dangerous, repetitive or runs around the clock, Electrek reported. Electrek also notes that Tesla's earlier public targets for Optimus production and external sales were set for earlier years than this one.

title: Danish grocer Føtex pilots Unitree humanoids for overnight restocking
summary: Føtex, part of Salling Group, has started a multi-year pilot with HIVE Robots to train humanoid robots to restock shelves after closing time, ESM Magazine reports.
body: Short answer: Føtex, the Danish supermarket chain that is part of Salling Group, has started a multi-year pilot with Danish start-up HIVE Robots to train humanoid robots to restock shelves after closing time, ESM Magazine reports. The first trials are at a Føtex store in Lyngby, north of Copenhagen, ESM says, citing Euronews.

According to ESM, the robot hardware comes from the Chinese developer Unitree, while HIVE Robots writes the control software and handles the machine learning. Trials run outside opening hours so the robots can be tested and data collected without shoppers in the store.

To gather training data, human operators wearing VR headsets and using handheld controllers guide the robots through tasks such as lifting bags of pasta onto shelves, ESM reports. The current prototypes work more slowly than human staff, and developers expect AI progress to speed them up, it adds.

Simon Kudsk, Føtex's operations director, is quoted as saying that stores are designed around customers moving through them, which makes conventional industrial robots unsuitable, and that a human-shaped robot can move around the store naturally. ESM adds that Salling Group says the aim is to support staff rather than replace them, that HIVE Robots is targeting commercial deployment by early 2027 under an hourly service fee, and that Kudsk estimates a full rollout across the chain could take up to five years.

title: Berkeley's SuperMimic trains a humanoid motion controller in three hours on one GPU, authors report
summary: UC Berkeley researchers report that SuperMimic matched a baseline humanoid motion tracker that trained for seven days on 128 GPUs, using three hours on one GPU.
body: Short answer: UC Berkeley researchers report that a method called SuperMimic trained a humanoid whole-body motion controller in about three hours on a single GPU, surpassing the return of a baseline tracker that, per the authors, trained for seven days on 128 GPUs. The claims come from the paper's abstract and the project page; the authors list it as a CoRL 2026 paper.

The method learns to imitate a large library of human motions, 129,514 in the benchmark. Instead of training only inside a physics simulator, it fits one learned world model to logged simulator data and trains the control policy together with it, using gradients from short imagined rollouts, the authors explain.

The authors report using more than 1,000 times fewer GPU-hours than the baseline and failing on 25 of the 129,514 benchmark motions, against 179 for the baseline's released checkpoint. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs they report zero failures. They also say one policy runs on a physical Unitree G1 robot, including acrobatic motions.

The authors note several caveats themselves: the runs used different hardware (one NVIDIA H100 versus 128 L40 GPUs) and different amounts of motion data, and the benchmark motions are training motions, so the failure counts measure coverage rather than generalisation to new motions.
analysis: Analysis: If the results hold up under independent replication, much lower training cost could let smaller labs experiment with whole-body humanoid control. That is our reading, not a claim made in the sources.
disclaimer: This article summarises a research paper and project page by its authors. The results have not been independently replicated by us. It is not advice of any kind.

title: NVIDIA expands Isaac robotics platform as Agile Robots unveils Agile ONE SN humanoid
summary: At GTC Berlin on 21 October 2026, NVIDIA announced additions to its Isaac robotics platform and Agile Robots announced the Agile ONE SN reference humanoid, according to NVIDIA.
body: Short answer: At GTC Berlin on 21 October 2026, NVIDIA announced additions to its Isaac robotics platform, and Agile Robots announced Agile ONE SN, a humanoid reference platform built on NVIDIA's Isaac GR00T software and Jetson Thor computer, according to NVIDIA's press release.

NVIDIA says the Agile ONE SN body stands 1.40 metres tall, weighs 40 kg and has 31 degrees of freedom, with two five-finger hands, head and wrist cameras, lidar and motion sensors. The companies say it is meant for humanoid research and development, scheduled to be available in early 2027, with planned integration of NVIDIA's Halos safety system. NVIDIA also claims the bundle cuts setup time "from weeks to days".

On the software side, NVIDIA says Isaac Lab 3.0 is now generally available and describes a new open-source Isaac OS runtime and a library of more than 2,000 simulation-ready robotics and factory assets.

title: Schaeffler opens Taicang factory where humanoids help build parts for humanoids
summary: Schaeffler says its new Taicang, China factory uses six humanoids to assemble joint modules, including actuators, for other humanoid robots.
body: Short answer: Schaeffler, the German motion-technology company, has opened a roughly 7,500 square metre "lighthouse" factory in Taicang, China, where six humanoid robots help assemble joint modules, including actuators, for other humanoid robots, the company said in a press release dated 20 October 2026.

According to Schaeffler, the six humanoids work across five stations on an assembly line the company developed. They stage and sort parts, join them, then inspect, label and package the finished modules. A digital twin mirrors the line in real time and logs measures such as assembly accuracy, step duration and energy use, so changes can be tested virtually before they reach the real line.

The site also holds a training and data-collection centre. Schaeffler says it trains humanoids there for tasks such as visual inspection, packaging, material handling, moving containers and line-side restocking, using set-ups modelled on conditions in its roughly 100 manufacturing plants. The company says the factory marks the start of mass production of these components for Schaeffler.

Schaeffler also says it added two customers from the Greater China region in the third quarter of 2026, lifting its global humanoid-robotics order intake to about 400 million euros. Gasgoo adds that Schaeffler Embodied Intelligence (Taicang) Co., Ltd. was set up in early 2026 to develop the site, and describes it as a platform for working with Chinese robotics companies.
disclaimer: This article summarises a company press release and one trade report. The order figure and production claims are Schaeffler's own and have not been independently verified. Schaeffler is a listed company; this is not investment advice.

title: Eka Robotics announces $150M Series A for force-sensing robot manipulation
summary: Eka Robotics said on 20 October 2026 it raised a $150 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and F-Prime; SiliconANGLE reports a $1.45 billion valuation.
body: Short answer: Eka Robotics, a robotics start-up, announced on 20 October 2026 a $150 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and F-Prime, a Fidelity Investments affiliate, according to SiliconANGLE and the company's announcement. SiliconANGLE reports a valuation of $1.45 billion.

Eka says it is building a "vision-force-action" model that combines camera images with force feedback from a custom gripper. It says the model is trained mostly in simulation using reinforcement learning, not by imitating human demonstrations, and that it is starting with dexterous manipulation, with examples such as packing fruit and assembling server racks.

The company reports its robots pick a wide range of objects not seen in training at about 1,500 operations per hour, against a human baseline of about 600 that Eka uses. SiliconANGLE adds that Eka told TechCrunch the robots handle objects up to one kilogram, succeed on more than 95% of picks, and are in pilots with industrial customers it has not named. These are company figures and have not been independently verified.

SiliconANGLE, citing TechCrunch, quotes Kris Hauser of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as saying a demo had a "wow factor" while questioning whether the system could run on an assembly line for a year without failure. He said it is still an open question whether it generalises beyond pick-and-place.

Eka says the new money will help extend the model to more tasks and speed up customer deployments. According to SiliconANGLE, the company was started last year by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and Tuomas Haarnoja, who joined from Google DeepMind, and investors have now put in about $161 million in total.
analysis: Analysis: Dexterous hands are widely seen as one of the hard problems for humanoid robots, so progress in force-sensing manipulation is relevant to the whole field. Eka's results so far are company-reported pick-and-place numbers, and independent, long-running trials would be needed to judge them.
disclaimer: This article reports a funding announcement. Valuation and performance figures come from the company and a news report and have not been independently verified. It is not investment advice.

title: China expects over 100,000 humanoid robots built in 2026 as first national standards approach
summary: A Chinese ministry official said China expects over 100,000 humanoids built in 2026, per China's SCIO; first national standards apply from April 2027.
body: Short answer: A senior Chinese industry ministry official said on 19 October 2026 that China expects to produce more than 100,000 humanoid robots this year, China's State Council Information Office (SCIO) reported. Separately, China's first six national standards for humanoid robots, announced in mid-October, take effect on 1 April 2027.

According to SCIO, Wei Wei, director general of the Department of Science and Technology at the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, told a Beijing press conference that China had developed more than 400 humanoid models by the end of June, with production above 40,000 units. He said products are being tested and deployed in more than 300 priority scenarios, including warehousing, logistics, catering, retail and household services.

The ministry plans to encourage retailers and other businesses to open their facilities to robot testing, to publish a 2026 edition of its guidelines for building a humanoid-robot standards system, and to set up a high-level open-source community, SCIO reported. Wei also said it will strengthen monitoring and testing of product quality, cybersecurity and data security while advancing ethical governance.

On the standards, CCTV reported on 16 October, citing the State Administration for Market Regulation, that six national standards were approved: five technical-requirements standards covering a humanoid's body, system architecture, environment perception and decision-making, plus one standard for simulation test platforms. MEKAWIRE, reading the national standards database, says they are recommended rather than mandatory, were issued on 28 September, and that Unitree, UBTech and Xiaomi's robot unit are listed among the drafters of all six.
disclaimer: Production figures and plans are official statements and forecasts, not guarantees. The standards are described from news reports and a database listing, not from the standard texts themselves. This article is not legal or compliance advice.

title: South Korea grants safety-rule exemption for 20 Robros humanoids in factory pilot
summary: A Korean regulatory-sandbox committee granted Robros an exemption so 20 of its humanoid robots can work near people at four companies' sites, Seoul Economic Daily reports.
body: Short answer: A South Korean regulatory-sandbox committee has granted the robot maker Robros an exemption from safety rules written for stationary industrial robots, so that 20 of its bipedal humanoid robots can work in spaces shared with or next to people at four companies' sites, Seoul Economic Daily reported on 14 October 2026.

The newspaper lists the sites as Nepes (semiconductors), Sungwoo Hitech (auto parts), HD Hyundai Samho (shipbuilding) and Delivery Lab (logistics). Tasks it names include removing contaminants from components, placing auto body parts, stacking scaffolding pieces and moving refrigerated packaging.

Before the exemption, the paper says, existing rules treated industrial robots as stationary equipment and required fences or other barriers between robots and human work areas. The exemption is conditional on risk assessments and safety measures, and data from the pilot is to inform future safety standards, according to the report.
Trade and Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan was quoted as saying that "AI technology is advancing so fast that regulation struggles to keep up".

title: Minerva Humanoids says it raised about $10M pre-seed led by General Catalyst
summary: San Francisco start-up Minerva Humanoids said on 6 October 2026 it has raised about $10 million in pre-seed funding led by General Catalyst, according to its press release.
body: Short answer: Minerva Humanoids, a San Francisco robotics start-up, said on 6 October 2026 that it has raised approximately $10 million in pre-seed funding led by General Catalyst, with Long Journey Ventures and Credo Ventures as co-leads, according to its press release.

The company says it is building humanoid robots for hazardous work in oil and gas and public safety. According to Minerva, its robot Roger is operated by trained specialists wearing VR headsets, while onboard software handles balance and navigation, and the company describes it as semi-autonomous.
Minerva names Sandor Felber as CEO and Maurice Rahme as CTO and says its first paid pilots begin this autumn. The release lists Hugging Face and Codecademy among other participants in the round.
